title: The Toolbox at the End of Your Arm

blocks.prompt: The Boss of Your Hand
blocks.text: Your thumb is not just a short finger. It is the boss of your hand. Look where it sits. It sits low, off to the side, and it can swing across to touch every fingertip. Try it. Now hold your thumb down against your palm and try to pick up a coin. It is hard. Keep it down and try to open a jar, or hold a pencil, or do up a button. Almost every job your hand does starts with the thumb. Most animals cannot do this. Your thumb is one big reason people can build things.

blocks.prompt: The Puppet on Your Wrist
blocks.text: Make a fist, then open it. That took twenty seven bones. Each hand has twenty seven of them: eight small blocky ones in your wrist, five long ones inside your palm, and fourteen in your fingers and thumb. Your two hands and two feet together hold more than half the bones in your whole body. Now look at the back of your hand while you wiggle your fingers. You can see thin cords sliding under the skin. Those are tendons. Here is the strange part. There are no muscles inside your fingers at all. The muscles that bend and straighten them sit up in your forearm. Wrap your other hand around your forearm and wiggle your fingers again. You will feel the muscles working there, a long way from the fingers they move. Your fingers are pulled by cords, the way a puppet is pulled by strings. The strings just happen to be inside you.

answers: twenty seven

(inference: fat muscles in the fingers would make them thick and clumsy)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fingerprints form before you are born
Identical twins have different prints
The ridges help you grip and feel
Wet fingers wrinkle on purpose
Koalas have fingerprints almost like ours

blocks.prompt: The Lines Nobody Gave You
blocks.text: Press a fingertip against a window and look at the mark you leave behind. Those loops and lines are friction ridges, and they cover your fingertips, your palms, and the soles of your feet. You grew them before you were born, around your fourth month in the womb, and the pattern has not changed since. It will not change for the rest of your life. Identical twins share nearly all of their DNA and still have different fingerprints, because the ridges are shaped partly by how the skin happened to fold and press as it grew. Nobody chose your pattern. It simply happened, once, and stuck. So why have ridges at all? Scientists are still arguing. One answer is grip. The ridges give your skin something to catch with, the way tread catches on a tire. Another answer is touch. Under each ridge sit nerve endings that read vibration. When you slide a fingertip across a surface, the ridges buzz, and that buzzing is how you can tell silk from paper without looking. Then there is the puzzle in your bathtub. Stay in the water long enough and your fingertips wrinkle. For years people assumed the skin was soaking up water and swelling. It is not. Your nervous system does it on purpose. Blood vessels under the fingertip narrow, and the skin above them puckers into channels. We know it is deliberate because people whose finger nerves are damaged do not wrinkle at all. The best guess is that the channels work like the grooves in a wet weather tire, letting water escape so you can still hold on to something slippery.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Precision grip: thumb pad to finger pad
Chimp thumbs are too short to oppose

blocks.prompt: The Grip That Built Everything
blocks.text: Close your hand around a hammer. That is a power grip: fingers wrapped, thumb clamped over the top, the whole hand working as a single clamp. Now pick up one grain of rice between your thumb and the tip of your index finger. That is a precision grip, and it is far rarer in nature than you would guess. A chimpanzee is several times stronger than you and cannot do it well. Its fingers are long and curved, built for hanging under branches, and its thumb is short and cannot reach past them. Human hands went the other way. Our fingers grew shorter and straighter, our thumbs longer and more muscular, until the thumb could swing across and meet each fingertip squarely, pad to pad. Anatomists call that opposition. It is the difference between grabbing something and handling it. Threading a needle, striking a match, tying a knot, and shaping a stone tool all live in that narrow gap between thumb tip and finger tip. Our ancestors gave up the ability to hang easily from a branch and got that gap in return. The brain paid for it too. If you map which patch of the brain's surface listens to which patch of skin, the map comes out badly distorted. The territory given to your hands is enormous, larger than the territory for your entire back and both legs together. Your back is huge and reports almost nothing. Your fingertips are small and report constantly, because they carry some of the densest touch nerves in the body. The hand is not just well built. It is heavily staffed. One more oddity. About nine people in ten write with the right hand, and no other animal leans that hard across a whole species. Individual chimps have preferences, but their groups split much closer to even. Whatever made us right handed seems tied to the way language settled into the left side of the human brain, which is the side that controls the right hand.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: 27 bones, no muscle inside the fingers
A saddle joint sits at the thumb's base
Friction ridges form by chance in the womb
Hand stencils are among the oldest art
Ten fingers, and math in tens
Sign languages have full grammar

blocks.prompt: The Hand That Made Everything Else
blocks.text: Whatever you build, you build it with a machine you did not design and cannot replace. It has twenty seven bones, more than thirty muscles, and not one of those muscles inside the fingers themselves. The engines sit back in the forearm and pull on the fingers through long tendons, which means the parts that do the finest work in the known universe are, mechanically speaking, puppets. Start with the thumb, because everything starts with the thumb. At its base sits a saddle joint: two curved surfaces nested crossways, like a rider on a horse. A hinge can only swing. A saddle can swing and rotate, and that rotation is the whole trick. It turns the pad of the thumb to face the pad of each finger squarely, so the two can pinch. Anatomists call this opposition. A chimpanzee, far stronger than any human, has a thumb too short to reach past its long curved fingers, so it grabs superbly and pinches poorly. Our ancestors traded away the ability to hang effortlessly from a branch and received, in exchange, the ability to hold a flake of stone at exactly the angle needed to strike another one. Every tool since has come out of that trade. The brain rebuilt itself to match. Map the strip of cortex that receives touch, and the body it draws is a monster: giant hands, giant lips, a back the size of a postage stamp. The hand claims more of that territory than the trunk and both legs combined, because it sends more information than they do. Fingertips carry some of the most densely wired skin on the body. Run one across a table and the ridges on it vibrate, and nerves underneath read that vibration as texture. You are not really feeling wood. You are feeling wood buzz. Those ridges are also, by accident, a signature. Friction ridges form before birth, shaped partly by chance folds in growing skin, which is why identical twins carrying the same DNA leave different fingerprints. Nobody designed them to identify us. They do it anyway. Perhaps that is why the oldest art on Earth is so often a hand. In caves in Spain, France, Indonesia, and Argentina, people who had no writing, no clocks, and no name we will ever learn pressed a palm to cold rock and blew powdered pigment around it, leaving a pale hand ringed in color. Some of those stencils are tens of thousands of years old. They are not pictures of anything. They are the exact shape of one specific person, held still, in one place, on one day. The message survives because it needs no translation: someone was here, and this is the shape of the part of them that touched the wall. The hand kept talking after that. We counted on ten fingers, which is the plainest reason so much of the world does math in tens. Deaf communities built entire languages out of hand shapes, with grammar as complete as any spoken tongue. We shake hands, we point, we wave. Long before a word leaves your mouth, your hands have started the sentence. There is a temptation to say the hand made us human. That is too neat. The hand and the brain built each other, slowly, over millions of years, and neither one gets the credit alone. But this much is fair: nothing you value was made by a mind by itself. Something had to reach out and touch it.
